opus-5.5.text:
I think the core idea is that right now we treat every example and every input as if it deserves the same amount of compute, and that's just not how the world works. Most of our training data is fairly redundant. A huge fraction of examples are learned early and easily, and then we keep paying to pass them through the full network, epoch after epoch. Meanwhile the long tail, the rare, noisy, or genuinely hard examples, is where a lot of the interesting learning and a lot of the failures actually happen.

So adaptive training, to me, is about letting the model or the training procedure decide where to spend effort. That can look like a few different things. One is data-centric: prioritizing or pruning examples based on some signal of difficulty or informativeness, so you're not wasting gradient updates on things the model already knows. Some of our work looking at which examples are hardest for compressed models found that pruning disproportionately hurts that long tail, which tells you those examples carry a lot of signal. If you can identify them, you can allocate more to them and less to the easy majority.

Another angle is conditional computation: architectures like mixture of experts, or early exiting, where different inputs take different paths and use different amounts of compute. That breaks the assumption that model capacity and compute cost have to scale together. You can have a very large model in terms of parameters but only activate a small fraction for any given input.

And I'd add that this matters beyond just efficiency. A lot of the field's progress has come from the bitter-lesson style approach of scaling everything up, but that's expensive and it concentrates who gets to do research. If we can be smarter about how compute is allocated, both during training and at inference, we get models that are cheaper, more accessible, and potentially more robust, because they're actually paying attention to the parts of the distribution that matter rather than memorizing the easy stuff over and over.

r001.rationale: The response says training treats every example as deserving the same compute, despite many being easy and redundant while others are hard.

r002.rationale: It discusses models allocating compute to difficult examples but does not attribute this learning strategy to humans.

r003.rationale: It mentions pruning and prioritizing examples, but does not frame pruning as a binary allocation between retained and discarded examples.

r004.rationale: It proposes using difficulty or informativeness to spend more effort on examples the model has not learned and less on examples it already knows, including as training proceeds.

r005.rationale: It presents mixture of experts as conditional computation in which inputs take different paths and activate only part of the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about adaptive training is that it starts from a pretty simple observation: not every example, and not every part of the network, deserves the same amount of compute at every moment in training. Right now we mostly train in this very uniform way. Every image, every token gets a forward pass and a backward pass, every parameter gets updated, and we do that for the full schedule regardless of whether the model has already learned what that example has to teach it.

And when you actually look at the data, it's wildly non-uniform. Some fraction of examples are learned in the first couple of epochs and the model basically never forgets them. Then there's a long tail of harder, rarer, or sometimes just noisy or mislabeled examples that the model keeps struggling with. A lot of my earlier work, for instance on how pruning and compression disproportionately hurt that long tail, really drove home that models have very different relationships with different slices of the data. So if you know that, the obvious question becomes, why are we spending the same compute on the easy examples at step one hundred thousand as we did at step one thousand?

Adaptive training is the attempt to actually act on that. It can take a few forms. One is at the data level: dynamically reweighting or subsampling examples based on signals like loss, gradient norm, or how often the model has already gotten them right, so you concentrate compute where the model is still learning. Another is at the architecture level: things like early exit or conditional computation, where easier inputs route through fewer layers or fewer experts, and you reserve the full depth of the network for the inputs that need it. And a third is over the course of training itself, growing the model or changing the capacity you're training as the task gets harder, instead of paying for the full-size model from the first step.

Where I get most excited is that this isn't just about saving FLOPs, although the savings can be substantial. It's that it changes the trade-offs we've accepted as fixed. Right now efficiency techniques like quantization or pruning tend to be applied after the fact, and they quietly sacrifice performance on exactly the underrepresented or difficult parts of the distribution. If instead the model is allocating its effort adaptively during training, you have a lever to protect that long tail rather than discard it. So efficiency and robustness, or efficiency and fairness, stop being in tension.

The honest caveat is that the signals we use to decide what's "easy" or "hard" are noisy, and if you get them wrong you can end up amplifying label noise or starving important rare cases. So a lot of the research question is really about which signals are reliable, how cheaply you can compute them, and how to make these methods work at scale without a lot of fragile tuning. But I think the direction is clearly right. The uniform, one-size-fits-all training recipe is a historical artifact of what was convenient, not what's optimal.

r001.rationale: The response says uniform training spends the same compute on easy examples even after the model has learned them, identifying equal exposure regardless of difficulty as inefficient.

r002.rationale: It does not compare model training with human learning or say people spend more attention on difficult material.

r003.rationale: It mentions pruning and compression, but does not frame data pruning as a binary allocation of training attention between retained and discarded examples.

r004.rationale: It proposes dynamically reweighting or subsampling examples based on learning signals, concentrating compute where the model is still learning as training proceeds.

r005.rationale: It describes conditional computation in which inputs route through fewer experts when they are easier, presenting routing among model components as adaptive computation.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to move away from treating every example and every part of a model as needing the same amount of computation. With a fixed training setup, we make a lot of those decisions up front. But what a model needs can change as it learns.

Adaptive training could let us allocate more computation to examples the model is still struggling with, or adjust which parameters we update at different stages. The hope is that you get more learning out of the same computational budget.

The tricky part is deciding what deserves that extra computation. A high-loss example might be informative, or it might just be mislabeled. And if you focus only on average performance, you could end up neglecting rare examples that really matter. So I’d want to measure both the efficiency gains and who benefits—or loses—from that allocation.

r001.rationale: It identifies treating all examples as needing the same computation as a fixed approach and proposes giving more computation to examples the model struggles with.

r002.rationale: It does not compare model training with human learning or say people spend more attention on difficult material.

r003.rationale: It does not describe data pruning or a binary choice between retained and discarded examples.

r004.rationale: It proposes shifting computation toward examples the model struggles with and adjusting parameters at different stages as the model learns.

r005.rationale: It does not mention mixture of experts or routing among model components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to move away from treating every example and every parameter as if they need the same amount of computation. Some examples are learned quite quickly; others require more work. If training can adapt to those differences, we could spend computation where it actually improves the model, instead of repeatedly doing work that adds very little.

The challenge is deciding what deserves that extra computation. A difficult example might capture something rare and important, or it might simply be noisy. So I’d want to measure efficiency alongside which capabilities we retain and whose data the model learns well. Getting to a good average score more cheaply is useful, but we also need to understand what that average might hide.

r001.rationale: It identifies inefficiency in giving every example the same computation despite some being learned quickly and others needing more work.

r002.rationale: It discusses allocating model computation across examples, but does not attribute human learning efficiency to giving difficult material more attention.

r003.rationale: It does not describe data pruning as a binary choice between retaining and discarding examples.

r004.rationale: It proposes adapting computation to examples, but does not say allocation should follow what is salient to learning as training progresses.

r005.rationale: It does not mention mixture of experts or routing among model components.
